utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, let's call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, do you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Julian Nicholls, assisted by Denise Gustin case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you all. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman and good morning to you all. And I also thank you for the revised list of witnesses which I very much appreciate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was sent both to you and to the Prosecution Your Honour, and I'm assuming the former Thursday rule is no longer in effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The rule remains in effect, but what you gave us today, or what you emailed us proves very much that there was indeed a need for the document because it was all changed. And then, of course, as we go along, every Thursday before, you confirm to the Prosecution and to the Court what the situation is. But at least we have an idea of what to expect. My apologies to everyone, to the public, for starting late. It was due to some rearrangement that we had to make to come in the courtroom. There is work going on having the door replaced outside. I have been asked to inform them if the noise disturbs us at any time. So if you feel disturbed, do let me know, and they promised to stop the works immediately if we tell them to. Bring the witness in, please, Madam usher. And we could, with your indulgence, knock off 5 minutes from the break, say, have a 20-minute break instead of 25 today to recover the lost 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could do that today, I do have a lot to get through today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I meant, for both breaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kalabic. We are proceeding with your cross-examination. Just take the opportunity of reminding you that you are testifying under oath on the basis of the solemn declaration that you entered yesterday. So please, take a chair. And Ms. Korner will proceed with her cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Korner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, yesterday I asked you a number of questions about who you had spoken to from the Defence team. Do you recall that? And can I please remind you, sir, just answer the questions yes or no if you can because otherwise assuredly you will have to come back. Now, do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In particular, I asked you about a gentleman named Milan Trbojevic, and you said you didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say I didn't know him. I said I didn't talk to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, I'm going to read back to you what you said yesterday, and this is page 82 of the LiveNote. You were asked who did you speak to? Was it Mr. Ackerman? You said no. Ms. Maglov? I can't remember the name of the person. "If I could see him, I would recognise him I'm sure." "So it wasn't Mr. Trbojevic, whom you know, presumably, Milan Trbojevic." "No, it wasn't him, and no, I don't know him." I'd like you to look please, now, at now Exhibit P2479. There's an English on the ELMO, and I'm going to hand the B/C/S copy to you. These are the minutes of the 20th session of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska held on the 14th and 15th of September 1992. And can you turn, please, in your document to page 9, and you'll see I've marked something. And if the usher could put page 7 of the English on the ELMO. Page 7 of the English. I'm sorry, if you turn the document you have been given to page 7 -- I see, the ELMO is not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't see anything on mine anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I see. Well, Your Honour, have Your Honours got the document with you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at page 7, does that show, Mr. Kalabic, that you that day were appointed to a constitutional issues committee together with Mr. Trbojevic, you being number 5 and Mr. Trbojevic being number 7?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is a mistake. This is not me. This is another person whose family name is Kasagic, not Kalabic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my fault. If you turn, please, to the following page, page 8, I marked that one by mistake, privatisation and denationalisation committee. Mr. Trbojevic being the chairman, you at number 4, and at number 5 Radoslav Brdjanin. Now, can you explain to us, Mr. Kalabic, why you told us yesterday you didn't know Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I didn't know Mr. Trbojevic. I know Trbojevic because he was a deputy in the assembly throughout the time I was a deputy. There must have been a mistake in the interpretation, so it turned out that I don't know Mr. Trbojevic. I do know him, but I didn't meet him concerning this Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your explanation is that the interpreters interpreting you yesterday, and I asked you twice about him, made a mistake. You never once intended to say you didn't know him?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that I don't know Mr. Trbojevic. I said I didn't meet with him with regard to this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're sure about that, are you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Ms. Korner, you could refer him to the section where you specifically reminded him where we're talking of the ex-minister of justice yesterday, and he still said he didn't know the person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question and answer went on as follows, Mr. Kalabic. I put to you: "You know presumably Milan Trbojevic." You said "no, it wasn't him, and no, I don't know him," according to our interpretation. Question: "All right, you don't know him. You don't know the minister of justice for the Republika Srpska or the ex-minister of justice for the Republika Srpska?" Then you said: "Maglov, I'm not familiar with that name." And I said: "No, Mr. Trbojevic." And you said: "No, I can't remember the last time of the person, and there's really no reason for me to say that if I knew him." Now, I'm asking you, Mr. Kalabic, was it Mr. Trbojevic who actually took a statement from you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't Mr. Trbojevic. I said that yesterday. And if I said that I didn't know the minister of justice, I had Mr. Maglov in mind. I had a long thought yesterday, and the statement was taken from me by a man called Peric or by a man called Bozic. I really can't remember the person's name because this was a year ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So it was a statement, was it? Somebody was writing down what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I can clarify this. No statement was taken from this witness. It was probably Mr. Peric that he talked to. At best there were notes made of that conversation which are just notes made by Mr. Peric taken. There was no statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If there would have been a statement, it would have been turned over.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hear what Mr. Ackerman says. Anyway, I want to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. You can hand that document back. Thank you very much, Mr. Kalabic. Now, Mr. Kalabic, you said on a number of occasions yesterday that your aim and the aim of the other members of the crisis staff was to preserve peace in the Municipality of Kljuc at all times between October 1991 and September of 1992. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried to preserve peace in Kljuc forever, not only throughout this brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can I take from that that the last thing that you or any of your fellow members of the Crisis Staff of Kljuc would want to do is provoke ethnic tension?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I object to the question. I don't think he's in a position to speak for all the other members of the crisis staff. She could ask him what he intended and whether he wanted to provoke tensions or not. But I don't think he can speak for what everybody else was speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I overrule you, Mr. Ackerman. The question is perfectly legitimate. He was part of the crisis staff, and he can or should be in a position to answer questions regarding the policy of the crisis staff. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you need to repeat the question because he didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would not want to, would you, Mr. Kalabic, provoke, that is, make matters worse between the various nationalities in Kljuc by speeches or actions that you took?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that I would not want to achieve such an effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your discussions with your fellow members of the crisis staff, did you understand that they wouldn't want to do that either?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My conclusion was mostly that all the other members of the crisis staff were eager to preserve peace at all costs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to have a look again at the document you were shown by Mr. Ackerman, Exhibit P861, and I will hand you a marked copy of the B/C/S. I don't know if the ELMO is working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a reason why the ELMO is not working, Madam Registrar? Is it maybe because it's not switched on or what?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The technician is working on that. But the video will capture it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. That's how we looked at the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could display the document from here, if it would be helpful to anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you find, sir, where I marked your name at the beginning of the speech that you made on the 29th of September. Can we remind ourselves on the 29th of September the war in Croatia had been going for about two months. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were problems because the Muslims and such Croats as you had in Kljuc were not responding to mobilisation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few Muslims did not respond to mobilisation at that time. More Muslims than not responded to mobilisation calls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you that there was a problem with mobilisation, and that as a result of that, there was already a rise in ethnic tension in Kljuc by September of 1991. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that at that time, no tensions existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the speech that you made again. You noted that this was the first occasion after World War II when we were actually reminded of the genocide which the Ustashas committed against the Serbian people. Rather late, but still in time to prevent history from repeating itself in its most horrible form, a foul war was being waged in one part of the country typified by the unleashing of a genocidal fascist hysteria on the part of the hoards controlled by and serving the goals of the pro-fascist and pro-Ustasha newly elected Croatian government. Are those the expressions you used, Mr. Kalabic, when you made this public speech?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have not put this sentence in the right context. At least, this is not what I have received in the interpretation. You have missed the point, the meaning of this sentence, the way you interpreted it. What I said was that a war is being waged in one part of the country. At least this is what the forces of dark are declaring, and they are serving the newly elected Ustasha government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were you using those kind of expressions, Ustasha, genocidal, fascist?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that time, this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I compared everything that was going on at the time with the year 1941, both sets of developments were happening under the same flag accompanied with the same symbols and involving the same players on the scene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But didn't you think that to use this type of language to an audience composed mainly, I suggest, of Serbs was likely to incite them to take action against their non-Serb neighbours?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not intend to achieve such an effect, and I'm sure I did not indeed achieve such an effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you and others like you, Mr. Kalabic, achieved just that effect, didn't you, because later on Serbs literally took action against their non-Serb neighbours?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not achieve that effect, and we did not take such action. Actions were taken on the 27th of May by the Muslim population in Kljuc, and not by the Serbian population. The Serbian part of the population reacted to whatever happened on the 27th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So everything that happened in Kljuc is as a result purely of Serbs reacting against what the Muslims did on the 27th of May? That's your evidence, is it, Mr. Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a very complex question which would require a lot of thinking, a lot of analysis, in order to -- for one to be able to give the right answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll come to what actually did happen in Kljuc later on. Mr. Brdjanin, while we're on the subject of rabble-rousing speeches, Mr. Brdjanin made some of the more extreme speeches, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally don't remember Mr. Brdjanin's speeches, but in those times, those times of conflict and the dissolution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, many politicians from all parties and all peoples often used very strong and vehement speeches. And this refers to all political parties and all nations, all peoples or ethnic groups, so that one could not actually find a high-ranking politician who did not speak in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I'm asking you not about what politicians from other parties did, I'm asking you specifically about Mr. Brdjanin. Did you hear Mr. Brdjanin make speeches which were extreme nationalist speeches?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has answered the question. He says I personally don't remember Mr. Brdjanin's speeches. He was asked the question. He answered it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but he then went on to say all politicians and all parties made it. So I'm repeating the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That means that you're now remembering any of Mr. Brdjanin's speeches. That's the only way I can allow it, Mr. Ackerman. But otherwise you are right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember any particular speech because these speeches all resembled each other. And all the politicians spoke alike so that I'm unable to remember a particular speech by someone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you as a politician used the same speeches, did you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a low-ranking politician. And of course I did not have an opportunity of giving speeches apart from this one instance that we have analysed, and this can be seen from all the documentation presented here yesterday, and you can see how I spoke and what I spoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a member, first of all, of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and thereafter a member of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic in Bosnia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend the assembly of the 12th of May 1992 in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the speech made by Mr. Kalinic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that speech. But recently I've had an opportunity of reading the speech in the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The speech, and I can hand you a copy if you like, in which he said - for the moment, I'm not going to give it to you unless you insist --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. A number of times I referred to it, and now I can't find it. Here, yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which he said: "Have we chosen the option of war or the option" -- usher, I'm not giving it to him. It's not on a document. "Or the option of negotiation. I say this with a reason, and I must instantly add that knowing who our enemies are, how perfidious they are, how they cannot be trusted until they are physically, militarily, destroyed and crushed which of course implies eliminating and liquidating their key people." Did you hear that? And Your Honour, I should have mentioned this is Exhibit P50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've seen it several times, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read this speech a few months ago in the daily papers. But until then, I did not remember it, and I think that at this session of the assembly, which was a very lengthy one, I went out quite often, as did other deputies, to the coffee bar or elsewhere, and I don't remember being present when Mr. Kalinic stated this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you remember whether you heard Mr. Brdjanin speak?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that either. Although I read those speeches, too, a few days ago. But I really don't remember that from the assembly session. I assume that I was not in the room at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're telling us is it just so happened that when the most extreme speeches were made, you weren't there. That's what you're telling us, is it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm trying to say. What I'm trying to say is that the assembly session was a very long one. Many speeches were made, many deputies often went out. They went in and out. And I did this, too, several times. So I assume that I was outside just at the moment those speeches were being made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you now, please, to look at Exhibit P35. I want to ask you about one of the sessions of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you'll have to get that one, usher, please. All right, we'll hand our copy over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was the session held on the 29th of February 1992, the day after there had been a session of the Serbian Assembly. Do you remember that? There had been argument about the declaration of an independent Krajina state, or a Republic of Krajina. Do you remember all that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me some time to look at the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you look at the document, do you remember there was an argument which started in the Assembly of the Serbian Republic about the declaration of an independent Krajina Republic. Do you remember all that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well -- all right. You read through the document.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend that meeting which was attended, as we can see, by Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did attend that meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to look, please, at the very last conclusion, number 3. It comes just before the vote which reads: "Establish immediately strict control of the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." I'd like you to explain to us, Mr. Kalabic, what was meant by that.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that anyone debated this issue at the meeting, and I can't remember that such a conclusion was adopted at all at that meeting, "establish immediately strict control of the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina" that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it to do with a discussion about making sure that control of the whole Krajina was in the hands of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you were there, Mr. Kalabic. This was perhaps one of the most important meetings, wasn't it, held of the autonomous region assembly? Are you really saying you have no recollection at all of what this conclusion referred to?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, what was most important was to agree on the constitution and to see the situation of the autonomous region in that constitution of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And those were the issues debated that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, are you saying that this conclusion, "establish immediately strict control of the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina" had no discussion at all and was just put in like that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that what you have just said is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You can hand that document back. Thank you. Now, I asked you yesterday whether you had been to a meeting in the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo, and you said you went on some occasions, but you couldn't remember when. I'd like you to have a look, please, at a receipt which is part of 2368. Is that you staying in the Holiday Inn on the 14th of February and leaving on the 15th of February?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my first and last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember attending a meeting at the Holiday Inn on the 14th of February in which Mr. Karadzic made a long speech?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended meetings at the Holiday Inn on several occasions, and I think that Karadzic attended all of those meetings. Without documents, it's very hard for me to remember one particular meeting on one particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to show you now marked already the record of the speech. This is P2383.14. Can you look at the part which is highlighted in yellow. Part of a very long speech made by Mr. Karadzic. And in the midst of that speech, he said this: "I have to say that we must get the last drop of power into our hands wisely, in unison with devotion and sacrifice in a humane way, of course, justly in a humane way, towards both the Muslims and Croats who live there. That is especially important, that they should not escape from our territories, but so that not a bird can enter without our knowledge, that is, if you remember, level 2. Do you know what I'm talking about?" "We do, yes." "So that is step number 2, the second level in smaller or bigger variations but that is what you must follow now slowly. You must have absolute control over who passes along your roads. What vehicle they drive, for what purposes. At your disposal, you should have above all the legal organs, the reserve police, and the regular police that must engage in service according to the order of civilian authorities because most municipalities have civilian authorities." Now, in that speech, I suggest to you, Mr. Kalabic, Mr. Karadzic was saying two things in this part of it. First, that you should move on to the second stage of those instructions. And second, that the police must act according to the instructions of civilian authorities. Do you agree that is what he was saying?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I can't remember the details of his speech. But that's what it says in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go back to Kljuc and say that the second stage of those instructions had to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back to Kljuc, but I did not see this as imposing a necessity of carrying out the second stage of the instructions, especially not in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because the reasons that the Bosniaks, the Muslims left the assembly, as they themselves said in the document you looked at yesterday, Mr. Kalabic, I suggest, is because it was abundantly clear that you, the Bosnian Serbs in Kljuc were preparing to seize power? That's why they left, wasn't it? Nothing to do with construction.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that's not the way it was. They didn't walk out because of that, because in practical terms, the Serbs and the Muslims were sharing power in Kljuc. And yesterday, I explained this division of power after the elections, and that's how it continued, until the 27th of May 1992. At a certain point, they walked out of the assembly, and in their communique, they said they had walked out because of illegal building. But three or four other reasons were given as to why they didn't want to attend the assembly. And those reasons are very important. Illegal building construction could not be a reason for anyone to walk of the assembly and not come back again. There is a document, a communique of theirs, which contains four other reasons. And if you wish, I will find it for you. And they listed those in their communique. After that, most of the assemblymen signed that communique. I'm referring, of course, to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, everybody can read what's in Exhibit P870, and I'm not going to take you to it. But the situation in Kljuc was this, wasn't it: That the Muslims and Serbs were almost an identical proportion of the population in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs had a slight majority over the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you said exactly, after the multiparty elections, there was virtually a sharing of power?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what I'm suggesting to you, Mr. Kalabic, is that it became abundantly clear by the beginning of 1992 that you, the Serbs, were proposing to take over complete control.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not proposing to take over complete control. We did not need complete control. What we needed in Kljuc was agreement, negotiations, not the rule of the Serbs over the Muslims in Kljuc. The conflict broke out because the Muslim politicians at the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc wanted a decision to be passed on the implementation of the referendum for a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Serbs were afraid of a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this was quite different. There was an article according to which two nations, any two nations under that constitution could outvote the third one. And there was a mechanism to prevent this. However, if someone wanted a decision to be adopted on implementing the referendum, they would first have to amend the constitution. The constitution was not amended. It was disregarded, and such a decision was adopted, and they wanted us to agree to this, to adopt this decision at the assembly. The assemblymen of Kljuc did not want to agree to this without an amendment to the constitution. That was the essence of the issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. By the time that the referendum was discussed, had you, the Serbs in Kljuc, voted in the plebiscite? Can you just answer yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I think the answer is not complete if I just say yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you can keep it short, what else do you want to say?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs considered that it was necessary to have a plebiscite among the Serbian people to see whether they were in favour of such a change or not. Or rather, to see if they were in favour of the implementation of such a referendum because all the peoples had to participate in reaching decisions of this nature. A plebiscite, or rather a referendum is something that all three peoples have to vote at. A plebiscite was to express the opinion of one single people. And at the plebiscite, the people said they did not want such a referendum because they were afraid that the fundamental interests of the Serbian people would be damaged by this, and that's why we had the plebiscite. We thought that if we had the plebiscite, there would be some forces in the world who would realise that the constitution had to be amended before the referendum could be held. That's my explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just finish up this subject, please, and could you just answers these questions, please, yes or no. The Serbs in the Municipal Assembly in Kljuc refused to allow a referendum or to assist in the setting up of the referendum in Kljuc. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that your question contains two questions, and that's why it's difficult to answer with yes or no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, did you refuse to lend any assistance to the mechanics required for the holding of the referendum in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were asked to adopt a conclusion on the implementation of the referendum at the assembly. And there was a standpoint from the Kljuc SDS Executive Board which stated clearly that the Serbian people would not take part in the referendum, but that we would in no way hinder the implementation of the referendum in Kljuc publicly and peaceably. And that's what is stated in the document and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you put out warnings on radio and by way of leaflet to prevent the Serbs taking part in the referendum. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. Already at the plebiscite, the Serbs said they would not vote in a referendum, so this issue had already been dealt with. There was no need for us to influence anybody not to vote in a referendum. Serbs could individually vote in a referendum if they so wanted. We did not prevent them from doing so. We did not prevent the referendum from taking place. We said that the referendum could be held peaceably, publicly in the same premises where such events were usually held on issues that were of local importance, so we did not try to talk anybody into voting, and we also did not prevent anybody who wanted to vote in the referendum at all costs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, I want to move on, but I want to make it absolutely clear to you. I suggest that is not right, and that indeed everything was done that was possible to prevent the Bosniaks from having this referendum. But can we move on, please. Could you look now, please, again at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what was that? Was that a speech, or was that a question, or what was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean, I have to put my case to this witness. I can't put a long answer like that go without making it clear that's not what we accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then you have to give him a chance to respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But he already had responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You can't make a speech like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed. In my system, that's perfectly acceptable. So I'm not surprised that Ms. Korner proceeded that way, and I'm not surprised that you stood up either. But let's move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, could you look, please, at 876 again that you were shown yesterday. B/C/S for the... I want you to turn, please, to -- this is the meeting you were shown of the SDS in Kljuc on the 18th of February. And you were asked about this speech you made yesterday saying all party members from distanced themselves from Vinko Stupar. All I want to ask you is this: What did you mean by the words after you said: "As for the division of Kljuc into cantons, it will proceed as we agree, but we shall not give up anything that is ours." What did you mean by that? You read this yesterday, Mr. Kalabic. What did you mean by the words: "We shall not give up anything that is ours"? Is there a problem, Mr. Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there isn't. What I meant was if Stupar's idea were to be carried out, then we had to be careful. So if such a thing was to happen, then we had to make sure that if the cantonisation were to take place, that each people should be given what they are entitled to. So if this was to be done, there should have been a previous agreement. Although it was a priori rejected, what Mr. Stupar proposed at one of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you consider that you were entitled to as the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant it was our general opinion in Kljuc that we were entitled to a joint life with Muslims and Croats in Kljuc Municipality, that we were entitled to peace, and that we were entitled to promote our national interests through the existence of some sort of a Yugoslavia. This is what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So nothing to do with land that you considered to be Serbian for whatever reason?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely never reduced myself to thinking what piece of land was Serbian, what piece of land was Croatian, what piece of land was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So if other politicians, for example let's take Mr. Klickovic in Krupa talked about that, that wasn't something that you considered was a proper thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there's two questions there. I think it's perfectly okay to ask him if that's a proper thing, but I don't know that he knows whether Mr. Klickovic ever said anything about that or not. If you said yes to that question, he'd be agreeing that Mr. Klickovic spoke of that. And I hope he knows that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present at the 12th of May assembly when Mr. Klickovic spoke about that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Mr. Klickovic's speech. At that time, I didn't know him all that well. We were just nodding acquaintances, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. As I say, I don't want to waste any more of my valuable time on this, so can you just give me the document, please. Now, is it your position that at the beginning of May you and Mr. Banjac and the two Kondics were still trying to maintain peace and harmony among nationalities in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were working on that, not only the three of us, because I don't consider myself as being one of the leading figures. It was the executive board of the SDS and the SDS and the deputies of the municipal assembly of both the Serbian ethnicity and of the opposition. All were working on this issue, on the issue of preserving peace in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe yourself as a Serb extremist?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you call yourself a Serb extremist, an extreme nationalist Serb?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have never been an extremist. I have never been a nationalist. To the contrary, I am convinced that I'm a peaceful, quiet, moderate person, and that I am a truly democratic person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe either Mr. Banjac, Mr. Kondic, Mr. Veljko Kondic, or Mr. Vinko Kondic, any one of those three, as an extreme nationalist Serb?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowing these people, I would really not use this term to describe their personalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like you to have now a look at a series of reports coming from the 1st Krajina Corps with whom you were familiar. First of all, Exhibit P898. We've marked the B/C/S, paragraph 6. It's a report dated the 4th of May. It's on the second page of the English. The state of morale. "We will elaborate on the state of combat morale in more detail in our report for the month of April, while we stand completely by the assessments we have made in our reports so far. "Could you please intervene through the Krajina government to exert its influence on representatives of the authorities in Kljuc. Serbian extremism is increasingly present there induced by the official organs of authority since the president of the municipality is asking to have his own army which he would use as he sees fit. This must be resolved urgently." The president of the municipality was Mr. Banjac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kljuc, the president of the municipality was Mr. Jovo Banjac. However, I never heard of such statements from Mr. Jovo Banjac. I see this document for the first time. I assume that it was drafted based on their assumptions, their views, or the needs that they felt at the time when they were drafting this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, you knew Colonel Galic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first met Colonel Galic - I can't remember the date - but it was in the barracks near Mrkonjic Grad. The name of that barracks is Kula, and it was not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you, please, Mr. Kalabic, because of the time. I want to know simply in May of 1992 did you know Colonel Galic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 27th of May, in the office of the president of the municipal assembly, we got acquainted a bit better. Up to then, he was just a colonel, and I was a small-time politician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you then tell us who in your view Colonel Galic was referring to as the "official organs of authority who were encouraging or inducing Serb extremism"? Or is it your view that Colonel Galic has got this completely wrong? There was nobody like that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the official organs of the government were President Jovo, vice-president Pilipovic, the president of the Executive Board Egrlic, and the vice-president of the Executive Board Tihomir Dakic. And I really can't specify who Colonel Galic was referring to. Was he referring to the administrative powers or just one part of the authorities?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't, in fact, Mr. Banjac attempting to, as it's stated here, have his own army?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You can hand that document back. I'd like you to have a look at a document from the next day, please. P889. I'm sorry, 899. B/C/S highlighted. This was actually addressed to the 30th Partisan Brigade, and I accept you wouldn't have seen this before. Under his -- from -- for General Talic, under "order," two, "submit a detailed report on the aim of the demonstration of Serbian extremism in Kljuc and Donji Vakuf and to what agree it was initiated by official organs. The deadline for this is 1000 hours on 7 May." What demonstration of Serbian extremism had taken place in Kljuc on the 7th of May? Mr. Kalabic.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me some time. In this document, I don't see that there were any demonstrations. At that time, there were no demonstrations. And this document absolutely doesn't say that there were any demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Look, please, at the next document dated the 7th of May, DB273, please. And I'll hand over...

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document, there is, however, something that could be discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm sorry. If Mr. Ackerman wants to discuss it with you in re-examination, I'm sure he will, but I need to move on. Will you look, please, this is a combat report of the 7th of May. Paragraph number 3. "Situation on the ground - highlighted - the Serbs in the Kljuc Municipality region want to assert their authority over the entire area and are demanding that the battalions 3-1 of the 30th Partisan Division to carry out this task." What was happening, wasn't it, Mr. Kalabic, was that you, Mr. Banjac, and others were planning to seize complete control of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, your statement is wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to look in a moment what did happen on the 7th. You can hand that back, thank you. Finally on this topic a letter -- sorry, it's P902. It's a letter from General Talic dated the 8th of May addressed to the Autonomous Region of Krajina Assembly Banja Luka. "Dear sir," and then I'm going to skip the first two paragraphs. "We would have failed in these efforts had it not been for the high level of cooperation between the military and civilian authorities which we have no doubt shall continue." Read the letter to yourself, and then I'm going to ask you about this. Now, Mr. Kalabic, what General Talic says is there is a presence in the municipality of Kljuc of extremism and disregard for anything which is not Serbian. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. I really did not know these people, and I could not influence the positions of either Mr. Talic or anybody from the army, so somebody from the security perceived the situation in their own way and drafted letters. Sometimes letters were written in order for people to create certain positions in the army. I see this for the first time, and the situation in Kljuc was not like this. Mr. Jovo Banjac weighed 160 kilos. He didn't walk too well. He was over 60. And he was simply not such a person. And his command was out of the question. He could hardly move. These are just fabrications. Obviously, there was a problem when people were mobilised and when they left for the front line. It was a problem to keep people there for a longer time. People wanted to go home, to return home. And I believe that Jovo Banjac advocated a human approach to every single soldier, that he wanted them to be able to go home to visit their family. But as to Mr. Jovo Banjac and his army, it's ridiculous. Mr. Banjac did not have his army, and before this 27th of May in the territory of Kljuc there were no units that would be moving about, that would be Chetnik units, or anybody else's units for which we didn't know. So this is just a fabrication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can hand that document back. Now, let's have a look what did happen on the 7th of May, shall we, in Kljuc. Could you have, please, Exhibit P171.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a public announcement made by the Crisis Staff of the Kljuc Municipality. "The Crisis Staff of the Kljuc Municipality informs citizens that yesterday on the 7th of May certain changes have been made in the Kljuc public security station concerning uniforms of the police employees and the signing of a solemn oath." And then it goes on to explain that "the police will now be wearing berets with the Serbian flag; militia written in Cyrillic script. The Serbian flag will be displayed with the Yugoslavia flag as a symbol signifying the fact that Kljuc Municipality is now a part of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina and the Serbian Republic. "It is stated that the very fact of replacing the symbols will not threaten the livelihood the workers who did not sign the solemn oath", et cetera. And then it goes on to say: "Citizens of the Kljuc Municipality know that the Municipal Assembly reached the decision about it joining the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina. The Kljuc Municipality will automatically be obliged to implement laws and decisions reached by the Assembly of the Serbian Republic and the Assembly of the Autonomous Region." And it goes on to explain how the changes should have been implemented earlier. And if we turn over in the English: "All authorities in our municipality have postponed the implementation of this task until yesterday in order to ensure its realisation in the most peaceful way possible." "The Crisis Staff considers that after the implemented changes the authorities in the Municipal Assembly should continue with the regular work, but it is noted that all decisions will be reached and all jobs carried out in accordance with the regulations and decisions of the authorities of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina and the Serbian Republic." And then it goes on to invite all citizens of the Kljuc Municipality to accept the changes and so on and so forth. What happened on the 7th of May was that unilaterally you, the Serbs took over the municipality, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. The assemblymen from the Muslim bloc had already walked out and had established their own assembly and had established the Bosnian Municipality of Kljuc. This decision was a follow up, and it was based on the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which had already been adopted by the Assembly of the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina. Of all the municipalities in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kljuc was the last one to do so. We were the last. All the others had done it before us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't agree, then, that what happened on the 7th of May by replacing the uniform of the police, putting up Serbian flags, and making people take a loyalty oath was in any sense a takeover?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see if he is receiving. Can you receive me now in your own language? There is something wrong, usher. Could you help -- are you receiving interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I gently to repeat the question again, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't just say that to give you time to think, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not agree that what is described as happening in this document was a takeover?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. I've explained that the assemblymen from the Muslim bloc had established their own municipality. They held meetings. They issued statements from their own meetings, and you have them, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, Mr. Kalabic, you don't have to give the explanation again. You don't agree. Do you agree that, by this stage, there had been moved on to the territory of Kljuc a large number of military?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no troops transferred to the territory of Kljuc. The troops arrived only after the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, then, please, what the paragraph that starts: "Citizens are notified that the increased presence of armed forces on the territory of the municipality is by no means an attack on the freedom and safety of any of the nationalities." What does that refer to, then?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The increased presence of armed forces did not exist in the Municipality of Kljuc, if you're referring to the army, however, there was the police in Kljuc if that is what is referred to here. And the police had an increased level of readiness. They were guarding the key facilities, the municipal building. So I believe that what is referred to here is the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you have a look, please, at another document -- all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to stop here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we make it 15 minutes instead of 20, do you think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I usually get problems with --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we'll leave it 20 minutes, and then we'll see how it goes. Mr. Kalabic, we're going to have a short break of 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Ms. Korner, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We seem to have lost everybody now, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to have a look, please, at another document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, the AV is not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is missing?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: AV director, so we cannot broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is he or where is she?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: With the best will in the world, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to wait. And can anyone... It's okay. I see that there are no further problems: I see that there are no further problems. So I thank everyone for being so punctual. You may proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please, at Exhibit P633. I see the B/C/S is unfortunately on the back of... This is an undated order as far as we can see, but signed by Commander Colonel Basara. And we can see that it's some time before the 7th, 8th of May because under paragraph 7 it says: "Provide each soldier engaged on 7th, 8th of May with a cooked dinner on the 8th of May." If we look at the top, please: "Because of the newly arisen situation in the territory of the Kljuc Municipality, the takeover and declaration of the Serbian Municipality of Kljuc, which may result in interethnic clashes..." I ask you again, Mr. Kalabic, is not what happened on the 7th of May in Kljuc a takeover of power by you, the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This did not happen because both before and after it was Mr. Jovo Banjac who was the president of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That doesn't seem to answer the question, to me, at least. I don't know if you want to put it again Ms. Korner or to leave it. And the Trial Chamber will draw its own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to leave it, Your Honour. We could go on for quite a long time on this, but I want to deal with --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the answer sounds to me like he didn't understand the question because it didn't relate to the question at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if that is the case, I will repeat the question to him myself, and perhaps -- Mr. Kalabic, you were read over the first part, the introduction of that -- of this document which specifically refers to takeover of the Serbian Municipality of Kljuc. And it's being suggested to you that indeed there was a takeover by the Serbs of the Municipality of Kljuc. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The colonel, when he mentioned the words "takeover of power," probably meant changing the insignia on the police uniforms because that's the only thing that happened on the 7th of May. Nothing else happened on the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I suggest you proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this whole order, Mr. Kalabic, is concerned with placing troops in Kljuc. As was described in that communique that the crisis staff issued, there were large numbers of troops being moved on to Kljuc territory or around Kljuc territory at the beginning of May. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. And that's not what it said in the communique.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you were wholly unaware that brigades of the 1st Krajina Corps - it was still the 5th at the beginning of May - were being moved on to the territory of Kljuc and around Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I never knew that something like this happened. I did not see any brigades in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to be absolutely clear on this. It is your evidence, is it, that you were never told and never heard that troops under the command of General Talic's subordinates were being moved into and around Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about this. And I didn't see anything like that happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can give us that document back. Could you have back, please, Document Exhibit P51 that you were shown yesterday. This was the meeting with the presidents of the municipalities in the zone of responsibility of the division dated the 14th of May, two days after the assembly had been held. And as you've already agreed, you were present at the meeting. You're number 11 on the list. Now, can you turn to the part where Kljuc was discussed. And we'll have the English on the ELMO now. "After the partial takeover of power, the situation in the territory of Kljuc Municipality is relatively calm. At the time of the takeover of power, units from the 9th Corps, Laniste, and the 5th Corps (a battalion of the 6th Partisan Brigade and the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Partisan Brigade) were securing Kljuc." Mr. Kalabic, how did you manage to tell the Court about a minute ago that you knew nothing of troops being put into Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Previously, I said that an engineers platoon or regiment, excuse me, was transferred from Knin to the municipalities of Kljuc and Bosanski Petrovac. This engineers regiment was located on the border between these two municipalities in a commercial facility. And this regiment had arrived earlier, and it was there. As far as I know, it didn't go anywhere from that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll read you back your last answer. "I want you to be absolutely clear on this. Is it your evidence that you were never told and never heard that the troops under the command of General Talic's subordinates would be moved into and around Kljuc." "No, I didn't know about this and I didn't see anything like this happen." You did know, Mr. Kalabic, because you were at the meeting where it was discussed.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the document which says that it was agreed that these units should be transferred to the vicinity of Kljuc. If you think that Laniste is close to Kljuc or Kula, that's where certain units were. If the soldiers from Kljuc who were mobilised and went to the front at Kupres, if you're referring to that, then those soldiers were only at Kupres. Apart from soldiers who were on leave and came to visit their families in Kljuc, I really don't know anything about other troops, and I didn't know at the time. And that is my correct reply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you one more time: When you heard it being talked about at the meeting that units from the 9th Corps, the 5th Corps were securing Kljuc, what did you think that meant?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember now what I thought at that point in time. But certainly this would enhance security in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's page 35, line 14, 15 -- 14. It says "certain units." I'm told what he said was "the engineer regiment was," not "certain units were."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't the truth this, Mr. Kalabic, to your certain knowledge then and I suggest now, that the army and the police and the politicians cooperated in this takeover of power? Isn't that the truth, Mr. Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still abide by the statement that there was no takeover of power, but only changing of the insignia prescribed by the constitution of the -- of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this refers to insignia on police uniforms. To take over power, we would have had to replace the president, Jovo, and other officials in the municipal assembly. That, in my view, is who the authorities were, not the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Mr. Kalabic, because I expect every bit of your evidence to make sense, if it is being suggested to you that the Serbs took over power, it would make absolutely no sense at all to say that the first thing that they should have done is to replace themselves or to replace their leaders. If the Serbs wanted to take power and take over the municipality of Kljuc, certainly that would be the last thing they would do and not the first thing. And what this document says is that "at the time of the takeover of power..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I make it absolutely clear -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These three battalions or whatever they are were securing Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to make this absolutely clear. And I'm basing this -- I'm not going to show the next document, P746.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you, Mr. Kalabic, that over a period of three days, between the 7th and the 10th of May, the parts of the 1st and 3rd Battalions of the 6th Brigade, an intervention platoon, a police platoon, and a reconnaissance platoon all acted together in taking over power. And by that, I mean erecting these flags, guarding these buildings, everything that you've already mentioned. All done as a takeover of power to prevent the Muslims having any kind of say in the government or in freedom of movement. Do you understand that? Because that is what I am suggesting to you actually happened. That's what happened, isn't it, Mr. Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened was what I said. The police changed the insignia on police uniforms, and if this implies a takeover of power, then that's what happened. Mr. Filipovic continued to come to the municipal assembly. He would sit and talk to Mr. Jovo Banjac. There were conversations and negotiations that took place, talks. And I really had no information about certain units being around Kljuc, except for the ones I've enumerated. I know about Laniste. I know that the regiment was there. I know about Kula, between Kljuc and Mrkonjic Grad. There was a barracks there that had always been there and is still there today. As for army activities in Kljuc, I wasn't aware of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying, then, finally, because I want to move on, that you didn't hear this particular item on the agenda being discussed? It's either yes or no or I can't remember, please, Mr. Kalabic.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember what was said at that meeting. But I know there was discussion on several occasions on changing the insignia on police uniforms and I know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Kalabic. I'm talking about the meeting of the 14th of May attended by yourself, Mr. Banjac, and various other presidents of municipalities, and Colonel Galic. At that meeting, are you saying you did not hear Kljuc being discussed --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now that this topic was discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that Mr. Filipovic came to the municipal building to negotiate. He came to negotiate about what was going to happen to the Muslims, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That the Muslims were absolutely petrified as to what was going to happen to them, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims were organised, and I'm not sure that they were petrified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the moment that this takeover took place, the police, let's deal with them for the moment, they all -- all non-Serb police officers lost their jobs immediately, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody lost their job. Everybody [Realtime transcript read in error "everything"] was offered the opportunity of staying on. But only one Croatian policeman accepted the offer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They could only stay on if they took an oath of loyalty to the Serbian Republic. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That was required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why should Muslim police officers take an oath of loyalty to the Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not able to know this because I didn't take part in most of those issues in connection with the police. There was a hierarchy from the public security centre in Banja Luka going down to a police station such as the one in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you why a Muslim police officer should take an oath to the Serbian Republic. Do you understand the question, Mr. Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do understand the question, but really, I don't know how to answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 39, 2, the word was everybody, not everything. Everybody was offered the opportunity of staying on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. That makes sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the 7th of May, the situation was this, wasn't it: That you, the politicians, together with the police and the army were just waiting for an excuse to drive the Muslims out of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to look, please, now at P196. This is the minutes of the meeting of the crisis staff held on the 13th, 14th of May. For some reason, your name is in handwriting at the top. And it appears that you were -- and Mr. Bajic from absent from the meeting of the 13th, but there, presumably, on the 14th. The agenda: "Number one, adoption of decisions (conclusions) on behalf of Kljuc Municipality pursuant to the decisions of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff." Mr. Banjac informed the members of the conclusions adopted by the crisis staff on the 11th -- of the regional crisis staff on the 11th of May. It's right, isn't it, that both you and Mr. Banjac attended the meetings of the regional crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I attended the meeting or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I don't mean this particular meeting, but meetings in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of the regional crisis staff. Not of the Kljuc Crisis Staff, of the regional crisis staff. It's being suggested to you that you and Mr. Banjac attended those meetings on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Jovo Banjac was a member of the crisis staff as the president of the municipality. But I was not a member of the crisis staff, and probably it so happened that sometimes I would attend those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Item number 1 of the conclusions: "The deadline for the surrender of illegally acquired weapons will be extended until midnight on the 14th of May 1992." Now, do you remember that there was a deadline issued to the Muslims and the Croats, the few Croats in Kljuc to surrender weapons?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting when Mr. Jovo Banjac is reported as discussing, I can't remember this conclusion at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. There was, was there not - leave aside the -- this particular meeting - a deadline issued to the Muslims and Croats that they had to surrender weapons to the police?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm confused, perhaps. I can't see where this says "Muslims and Croats."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, there you are, right, but the question is what it is. It's being suggested and put to the witness that the decision applied only to Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I really object to these type of objections because he's giving the witness the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think she was trying to get the witness to believe this said Muslims and Croats, and it -- when it doesn't say that. And if she was misleading the witness, it's perfectly proper for me to point it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness knows how to read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, in Kljuc over the radio and by other means a deadline for the surrender of weapons was given, was it not, to Muslims and Croats? And to make it absolutely clear, and not to Serbs. Mr. Kalabic, this has got nothing to do now with the document, I'm asking you now generally whether as a resident of Kljuc --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember. I don't remember any such thing. At that time, I really don't remember that this happened at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't remember. In other words, let's make this clear: You're not aware or you don't remember that a disarmament of -- that a disarmament took place in Kljuc at any time? Around about the period we're talking about? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was disarmament in Kljuc after the 27th May, not before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And was that the disarmament of Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody who possessed illegal weapons and military uniforms were asked to return them. That was one of the orders of the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only people, Mr. Kalabic, who were ordered to surrender weapons or made to surrender weapons were the Muslims and Croats. That's the truth of the situation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as we can see from item number 2, you were present at this meeting because you and Mr. Banjac advised the members of the crisis staff of the positions on the security situation in Kljuc Municipality. Do you remember what you said there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I really attended that meeting. But even if I did attend it, I did not engage in any discussions there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What does item 2 say?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Help me find the item that you're talking about. Is that one of the conclusions?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before we get to the conclusion under item 2, do you see your name?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, give it. Usher, if you give it to me. It's just under the -- it's shortly under the highlighted section. Item 2, AD 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to become more proficient in the language, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's actually about six lines under the highlighted Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 22624 to 22635. portion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, I don't want to spend --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember having said anything about this issue in this part of the meeting. But I suppose that the president did. He was the leading figure in Kljuc, and he was a member of the crisis staff. So...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were just an unimportant member, were you, Mr. Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the crisis staff in Banja Luka. Mr. Jovo Banjac was. I would only sometimes, very rarely, attend one of its meetings. So I was not a member, either a valuable or an invaluable member. I was simply not a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kalabic. If you very rarely attended and you weren't a member, how could you possibly tell the Court yesterday: "The decisions of the crisis staff, the regional crisis staff, if they existed, did not reach us in Kljuc. And we did not implement them." Page 74 of yesterday's LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the situation in earlier times. We saw a telex with a document which had never reached us. And this document serves to prove my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, are you really -- are you making these things up as you go along?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That is a proper question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I object to it. It might be a proper question, but I have an objection to it. First of all, I think the witness has become confused. I think he may believe the document he is looking at is from the Regional Crisis Staff and not the Kljuc Crisis Staff. And the question and answer immediately preceding this current one, I think, is clear that the question and the answer are totally unrelated to each other, and I think it deals with confusion. So that's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, objection overruled, Mr. Ackerman, but I will try and help your witness. Mr. Kalabic, let's bring this to an end. Yesterday, you made a statement to the effect that you wanted to make us believe you in stating that the decisions of the crisis staff of the ARK, the ARK Crisis Staff, couldn't have even been implemented in Kljuc Municipality because they never reached you over there. Now we have a document which is essentially a Kljuc document in which you are also reported to have been at least partly present which specifically refers to decisions taken by the ARK Crisis Staff and the implementation in the Kljuc Municipality. And it's being suggested to you that you're trying to hide something from us or that you're trying to go around in circles not to answer a question which is being put to you as the obvious. What's your position? You have in front of you a document which specifically would convict what you stated yesterday. Yesterday, you didn't say "we did not have reports on what's being decided by the ARK Crisis Staff before this date, but we had them afterwards." You just said that you never had them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct that during a certain period of time those conclusions from the ARK never reached President Jovo Banjac, and therefore they could not be considered because one document proved that they arrived by way of telexes, and this telex was never handed to Mr. Jovo Banjac.
