This specific document that we are discussing now is probably something that Mr. Jovo Banjac brought from Banja Luka from this meeting, and I'm sure that on the 13th and on the 14th, the crisis staff meeting was held in the municipality, and it is obvious that I was not present at that meeting on the 13th. Whether I was present on the 14th, I can't remember. But even if I was present, there was no reason for me to engage in any discussions or to inform members of the crisis staff about the decisions passed by the regional crisis staff because there was a person there who was a member of the crisis staff. So it was his duty to do that. That's probably why I cannot remember the specific date and the specific document and the specific conclusions. This is my answer, and I don't see any other reason for me to say anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you accept that the document shows that you were there and that you spoke?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say anywhere in the document that I spoke, or at least I haven't been able to find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Hand me the document back, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even if you give it to me, I will mark it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't, Your Honour, I really -- I'm concerned that -- I still have a lot to get through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please, have a look at a document six days later, P203. Do you agree this bears the stamp of the Kljuc Municipality and it's signed, this document? Mr. Kalabic, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a stamp, and the document is signed. Not by the president, Mr. Jovo Banjac, but by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Does that say that "at the meeting of the 20th of May 1992, the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region adopted amongst others the following conclusions," and it sets out four conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is absolutely unclear to me because the heading says that this is the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region from Banja Luka, and the stamp is that of the Kljuc Municipality, and the signature is of somebody who is not President Jovo Banjac. It is impossible for a document originating from the autonomous region to be stamped with the stamp from the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because, Mr. Kalabic, what was happening was the Kljuc Municipality was publicising the conclusions reached by the Autonomous Region Crisis Staff, wasn't it, issuing its own document?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honours, it's in P227, it's item number 13 on the Gazette.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I refer you to the 20th of May meeting of the regional crisis staff as number 13, P227. That's what's happening, isn't it, Mr. Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that I am really not clear on this document. I cannot comment on it because in the heading, it says that the document is of the regional staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, Mr. Kalabic. Now, it will take some guts and some daring to tell me that this is the heading. Is this a heading, or is this the address of the person or persons or institution to which the document is addressed? I'm very surprised that a person of your intelligence and your education is confused by this document. Or could be confused by that document. A heading is a heading, and that is the details of the addressee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You can hand the document back, Mr. Kalabic. I want you now to have a look at P208, which you saw yesterday. Mr. Kalabic, you can give the document back to the usher. This is the document that you saw yesterday, so you don't need to read through it again because you also saw it with Mr. Ackerman before you testified. "Crisis staff meeting of the 27th of May 1992." You say that was the meeting where you were all shocked and -- I think I better find your exact words. "The people who attended this meeting - this is page 53 of the LiveNote - terribly afraid and felt great uncertainty. They displayed, or rather they knew, they bore enormous responsibility but they did not have the strength to take any action that might prevent the further escalation of negative events in the area of Kljuc Municipality." Now, leaving aside item number 1, which I'll come back to, item number 2 deals with the recommendation for the municipality judges and prosecutor. Item number 3: "Remove all non-Serbian personnel from positions which allow independent decision-making and securing property." I'll come back to that in a moment. "Disarmament of paramilitary formations is approved in accordance with the plan that will be proposed." Refugees. Regional funds. Recommendation of the regional crisis staff that minimum wage is accepted. War tax. Television. And then paragraph 10, which we have been through, and so on. Are you really saying these were the decisions that were made by this afraid, uncertain set of people? Do you understand what I mean, Mr. Kalabic? They're fairly mundane, boring decisions, the lot of them.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were decisions by the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As far as item number 1 is concerned, you say that -- this is what you said yesterday about it. "I have to admit that we suddenly realised that at one time, an autonomous region had been formed, and this autonomous region had a crisis staff. Not a single conclusion of the crisis staff was analysed by us, but in this situation, uncertainty, we put on the agenda the fact that we were giving legitimacy to the conclusions that we had never seen or read." Now, that answer, Mr. Kalabic, in light of the documents we just looked at clearly was not right, was it? You had been considering, you in Kljuc, had been considering the decisions and putting into effect the decisions of the regional crisis staff since the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was from the 13th or the 14th of May that the decisions of the crisis staff were considered by the municipal crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, you were doing the same here, weren't you? Putting into effect the decisions of the crisis staff meeting that had been held the previous day, the 26th of May, which is number 17 in P227? That's what was happening here. Wasn't it, Mr. Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the document which would speak of the session of the crisis staff which was held on the 26th of May. Is there such a document? I'd like to see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, well, there is such a document. The Court's aware of it, and I'm not going to take it out. Where in this whole meeting did you discuss the situation that had arisen in respect of Pudin Han?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th of May --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 27th of May, this meeting. The document you're holding.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a different story. The 27th of May, there was a session of the crisis staff in the evening. And obviously, we did discuss the entire situation which had arisen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So this meeting of the crisis staff has nothing whatsoever to do with the situation in, as it arose, in Pudin Han and other places? It was before these events were discussed; there was a separate meeting. Is that what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what events are you referring to? If you are referring to the events which took place on the 27th of May, we discussed those events at the crisis staff meeting which was held in the evening of the 27th May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So this meeting that is recorded here is not the meeting at which the events of the 27th of May were discussed. Is that what you're now telling us here?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not clear as to what meeting are you referring to, what date, what day, whether it was on the 27th or some other day. What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, the longer you go on like this, really, the longer you will be here. The document you are holding refers to a crisis staff meeting on the 27th of May 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I had this document in my hands when you mentioned the meeting on the 26th of May. That's why I wanted to be absolutely clear whether you're talking about the meeting which took place on the 27th May or some other date. On the 27th of May, the crisis staff did consider the situation in Pudin Han and Granice and Velagici, and the situation was considered. And at that meeting, after these events, conclusions were passed just as they are indicated here in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, so, are we back to the situation that you're saying there was one meeting of the crisis staff on the 27th of May and one meeting alone?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 27th May, there were frequent meetings of the crisis staff of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, I suggest you are deliberately playing for time. Was there, for the third time, just one meeting of the crisis staff on the 27th of May or more than one meeting on the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of May, there was one meeting, but that meeting started late in the afternoon and ended in the early hours of the morning. There were certain interruptions in that meeting. There were breaks. Information was being awaited. So this was not all that simple. There was one meeting, and that meeting lasted a long time and had several breaks. It was on the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. During the course of that long meeting, the crisis staff reached all the decisions that are listed here. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are the decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the decisions that was reached was that all non-Serbian personnel were to be removed from positions which allow independent decision-making and securing property. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the conclusion under 3. However, there was no need to implement this decision because on the 27th of May, almost no Muslims turned up for work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest the Muslims who didn't turn up for work on the 27th of May is because blockades were being thrown up.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this assertion is not correct. There were no barricades on the roads, at least not to my knowledge. As a forestry engineer, before the 25th of May, that is, before the 27th of May, a day or two days before that, I passed through Pudin Han to Krasulje, and on the public road I did not notice a single barricade anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thereafter, all non-Serb employees were dismissed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, or rather, on the 27th of May, no one -- or that is the majority of the Muslim employees failed to turn up for work. But some 10 or 15 days after that, no one came to work, including Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. Because chaos prevailed in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I'm sorry, Mr. Kalabic. I'm going to ask you this one more time: Are you saying that not one single Muslim or Croat, although there were few Croats in Kljuc, was dismissed from employment?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After these events, most Muslims did not come to work at all. They simply did not turn up for work. Whether later on they were dismissed, I don't think so, because practically no one came to work. I remember well that where I worked, a number of Muslims arrived and picked up their salaries, which they had earned previously, and they had no problems with this. And they were even invited and asked to return to work. But out of fear that something might happen, people did not go to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You can put that document away now, and I'm going to ask you to look at part of Exhibit P8 -- I'm sorry, 989, which is the book of minutes from the Kljuc Assembly. I just want you to have a look at the record for the 1st of June. I've marked the part that I want you to look at. It's page 7, and then page 8 in English. These are the minutes from the Kljuc Crisis Staff session of the 1st of June. And if you go to where I've highlighted, if we turn over the page, does that say: "Veljko Kondic" -- and it says Rajko Kolobic. Is that you? Is it Kalabic in the original?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this is me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Were sent to attend the Krajina Crisis Staff session." It's right, isn't it, Mr. Kalabic? You were an active participant in the crisis staff in Kljuc and attended the meetings of the regional crisis staff on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has been asked the question. I think he answered it, that he went occasionally but was not a member. I think he has said that two or three times now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer again, Mr. Ackerman, because this is a crescendo, as you can obviously understand. As we go along, he's being shown documents with a view to making him agree that he was more important or he played a more important role than he has actually been portraying to so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document doesn't say anything different from what he said. This just confirms what he said, that he on occasion he would attend the Krajina Crisis Staff meetings but that he was not a member. This just confirms what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, please. Or Mr. Kalabic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, this clearly indicates, doesn't it, that you were an important, functioning person as a liaison between the municipal and the regional crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't show this. Together with Mr. Kondic, at this meeting, I was given a one-time task, so you need to read three lines before this "to go to Banja Luka and try to solve the problem of the telephone lines and to try to solve the possibility of communicating by teleprinter." Because the telephones in Kljuc had stopped functioning. Mr. Veljko Kondic was the director of the Kljuc post office. And the crisis staff tasked the two of us with trying at the main post office in Banja Luka to resolve the issue of telephone lines in Kljuc. This was a specific and one-time assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You can hand that back. Now, let's have a look, shall we, at dismissals, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you see how important it was for the witness to answer the question, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please, again at P974. Now, you were shown this document yesterday by Mr. Ackerman. And it's a letter addressed to the municipal assembly. In fact, information on managerial and executive staff. "We are sending you herewith information about the managerial and executive staff of Muslim and Croatian nationality holding positions of foreman and higher, et cetera." Companies had been asked, hadn't they, after the 1st of June to provide information about their Muslims and Croatian employees who held managerial positions?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there was no -- if nobody was going to dismiss them, what was the need for that information? Mr. Kalabic, if nobody was going to dismiss these people, why was that information required?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crisis staff decided this, and I really think that at the time we did not discuss any dismissals. But probably the prevailing opinion was that it was necessary to know where people were working, what jobs they were holding down, and what kind of security could be expected in the future from these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of these people lost their jobs, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, if you look at number 1 and 2 from the administration services, when all the others, or rather some of the employees who were not active in the army returned to their workplaces, these people also returned. Number 2, Draganovic also returned to his job. Sip is a large organisation. So I don't know all these people. Amra Mrsic also continued working for a time. Mile Belajic is a Croat, and he continued working until he retired. I think he retired in the second half of the war. And this is what I know. Besim Pudic also worked in Kljuc. He's under number 9 here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting to you is sooner or later, each and every one of them lost their jobs with this particular company. That's what I'm suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's answered the question. He's gone through the whole list and said that's not true. That some of them stayed there the entire time, some of them retired. He's answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the question is sooner or later, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I take number 1. Mr. -- Mr. Pobric lost his job and ended up working as a cleaner, didn't he, in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's the work he did. I think he was employed in the army to work in the rear. He was never a cleaner in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you look now, please, at 983. There should be a number of documents. Does the first one show that the crisis staff dismissed Nermin Kapetanovic as a judge?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, after the events of the 27th of May, like all the other Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, did not turn up for work for about ten days. And later on, when these people did return to work, he absolutely did not show up for work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next one, is that Dzemal Botunic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his case is the same as that of Mr. Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well then I'm not going to go on with this. You say dismissed because they simply failed to turn up for work.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they didn't turn up for work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you then have a look at, please, P1000. Is that a decision of the war presidency on the 21st of July which states in the clearest possible term only officials of Serbian nationality can occupy managerial posts, posts which may provide access to information, or involve protection of public property, and posts which are important for the functioning of the economy? And then it reads: "To all socially owned enterprises, joint stock companies, state institutions," et cetera. And that meant, didn't it, that no non-Serbs could hold any kinds of job?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is it possible to get such information? Yes, that was the decision, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't understand either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "where is it possible to get such information"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood the second part of your answer. But I join Ms. Korner in asking you to explain the first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, paragraph 1 doesn't say "every non-Serb." It talks about managerial positions with regard to particular information. That's what his answer was about. And her question was all non-Serbs, and he said, no, just those involved in -- where this information was involved. I think that's what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, what -- the first part of your answer was: "Where is it possible to get such information"? And then you said proceeded to say yes, that was the decision, yes. What did you mean by the words "where is it possible to get such information"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, posts which were important for the functioning --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Wait, wait, wait. The Judge asked a question. I think he deserves to have his question answered before Ms. Korner interrupts you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like to see -- are you taken by surprise by the document, Mr. Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have this document in my possession. This is the first time I'm looking at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But were you aware at the time of the decision taken by the crisis staff? Or is it all news to you in 2003?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the decision in this form. I can't remember the decision in this form. But there was something similar to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, yes, Ms. Korner, he's back to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, it's drawn widely enough, isn't it, to cover every kind of job, posts which are important for the functioning of the economy can be a man who chops down trees?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not know what Mr. Jovo Banjac meant when he drew up this conclusion, or rather this decision. As for a man who chops down trees, he would not hold down a post where he would be able to get important security information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. What it says is: "Can occupy managerial posts, posts which may provide access to information or involve protection of public property, and posts which are important for the functioning of the economy." You see, Mr. Kalabic, I make this as clear as I possibly can to you: My suggestion is all Muslims and Croats lost their jobs sooner or later in the Municipality of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they lost their jobs later, I cannot prejudge this. Whether they would have lost their jobs later. But I know that after the 27th, many of them failed to turn up for work, and that's the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest it's very, very far indeed from the whole truth, Mr. Kalabic. And I want you to understand very clearly that I'm suggesting that you're literally sitting here and lying to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I object to those kinds of comments. I think they're unnecessary and unwarranted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an obligation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. Let -- objection overruled. It's perfectly legitimate to put that to the witness, and it's up to the witness, then, to answer it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. Give him an opportunity to tell you I don't accept that, Ms. Korner, or I agree with you. I have been lying.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It does happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, it has been suggested to you by Ms. Korner that you are lying to us. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Ms. Korner, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After they had been dismissed, in order to leave the municipality if they hadn't been killed, they had to sign documents, didn't they, leaving their property to the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not dismissed. And those who left, who moved out from the municipality of Kljuc, with their family in order to preserve property from possible destruction, looting, torching, and so on was made over to the municipality. It became state-owned property, and this was done all over Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this was not something that was invented in Kljuc. It wasn't anything new in Kljuc. It happened in other municipalities as well, and it was simply copied from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree. It happened all over the Krajina Municipalities that were taken over like this, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Central Bosnia also, and other places, the same thing happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this period of time, did you put on a uniform?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my 26th year of age, when I completed my compulsory military service, on my return home when I was 26, I was assigned to a reserve police force. And from the date of the completion of my military service, I was a reserve policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you haven't answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was going to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, occasionally, I did put on a uniform, because from time to time I was assigned to war units and from time to time I went to the front lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about in the streets of Kljuc or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a time, at the very beginning, all the members of the war presidency, that is, the crisis staff, wore uniforms, and so did I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the decision, and I abided by it for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was the decision taken? Why should you, civilian members of the government, wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today, it isn't clear to me why the decision was taken. But the decision was taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you got yourself a weapon as well, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a member of the reserve police force, I was issued with a weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nothing to do with the police force, was it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the reserve police force. And from time to time, I went to the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm suggesting that the weapon that you acquired, Mr. Kalabic, had nothing to do with your membership of being a reserve policeman. Can you look, please, at P, first of all, 988. It's marked -- I have a marked copy of it in B/C/S. It's highlighted for you. Item -- It's minutes of the Kljuc War Presidency, 10th of July. And item number 2: "Decision allowing the war presidency members to move around in uniform and carrying weapons." You've told us I don't know how many times you weren't a member of the war presidency. So why were you moving around in uniform?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the crisis staff in the municipality became the war presidency, so that after the 27th of May I think -- I mean to say, officially it was named the war presidency. And I confirmed that as a member of the war presidency, on the basis of the decision, I confirmed that from time to time I carried weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You weren't a member. You've told us this. I think -- I don't know how many times, that you were not a member of either the crisis staff or the war presidency. So I'm asking why this decision had anything to do with you.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The autonomous -- I was not a member of the crisis staff of the autonomous region. That's what I said. And I said that Jovan Banjac was the president -- was a member, not me. And I was a member of the municipal crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He was shown the document to that effect yesterday, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like you to have a look, please, first of all, P1143, a part of thereof, and one which is a new document. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this was handed to Mr. Ackerman yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1143 -- no, no. Does that show that you, Mr. Kalabic, that you are confirming that you have received and signed for the following weapons: "One automatic rifle and 160 bullets"?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does the next document show that you've signed for a Russian-made machine-gun with 70 bullets?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was it necessary to have an automatic rifle and a machine-gun? Mr. Kalabic, why did you need both weapons?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I gave one of those weapons to someone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't that illegal?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that as a member of the reserve police force, I was given the task of giving someone this weapon. I can't remember the details, but I think that's how it was. Because really, I did not have -- except at the moment of being issued the weapons and handing them back, I didn't have two weapons at the same time. My weapon was this automatic rifle. .762.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask that the exhibit which relates to the Russian-made gun which has got the number in B/C/S 00574478 become -- I think it ought probably be attached to the first exhibit, so they're together, so it would be P1143.1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to come back. I'm going to deal with the events of the 27th and thereafter together. I want to come back to this report that you were shown yesterday, P1010, which is a report on the work of the crisis staff of the Kljuc municipal assembly. Before I do that, I'd like you to look, please, at P1009. And I'll give you the B/C/S. This is the minutes of the 13th session of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly beginning the 31st of July. Agenda: "Report on the work of the Kljuc SJB public security station. Report on the work and activities of the command of the 17th Light Infantry Brigade. Three. Report on the work of the crisis staff/war presidency." And I asked you yesterday whether this report would have had to have been delivered to the municipal assembly when the decisions are verified, and you said no. Do you agree now that you were mistaken?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say no. I said that the reports on the work of the crisis staff were subsequently in a later period submitted to the municipal assembly for verification. And this really proves and shows that this was on the 31st of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you accept - that's all I'm after - that this report that you were asked to look at yesterday was the one that was put to the municipal assembly on the 31st of July?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusions, the meetings, and the decisions of the crisis staff dating from the 27th May onwards were all put to the assembly on the 31st of July, and that's when they were all verified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Do you agree that -- have back the report, please. I'll give it to you, which is P1010. It's marked -- no, usher, please. Now, this is the report that I asked you about yesterday, and I already asked you about the paragraph that says that the municipal crisis staff in Kljuc considered the conclusions of the Banja Luka regional crisis staff binding. I want you to look, please, at the paragraph that's marked "During the armed conflict..." Which is on page 3 of the English. It begins: "During the armed conflict..." Do you see that? It's marked in yellow. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it highlighted?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So maybe he understands highlighted and is otherwise colour-blind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want to waste time. Can you give it back to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It has got two yellow lines down the side of it. Do you see that? "During the armed conflict, representatives, commanders, of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina regularly attended the Crisis Staff and War Presidency meetings. They commanded and carried out the war activities for the defence of the territory and citizens of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly against Muslim extremists. They cooperated and coordinated everything very well with the Crisis Staff of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly. All important and significant issues in the military and police domain were not resolved outside the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly. This period could be described as a period of very successful cooperation between the Crisis Staff and military bodies in defeating the armed resistance of Muslim extremists." Do you agree that's what's written there? Mr. Kalabic, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's an accurate description, isn't it, as far as the cooperation is concerned? That's accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that time there was cooperation. There was cooperation at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's turn to the events of the 27th of May. You were shown the document, the police document, that described the various incidents, and you said that all of them were accurate. Were you present at any of these incidents?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know yourself whether the descriptions you read were accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's just the form of the question, I suppose, that I'm objecting to. I was very careful in asking him "to your knowledge is this accurate," not "is it accurate"? To your knowledge, to your knowledge, to your knowledge. I think every question I asked him was "to your knowledge is it accurate," not a general is this accurate? But to his understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fair enough. But let the witness answer the question. It needs to be cleared up. But the point that you made is to be taken into consideration. So what I suggest is -- I don't think you need to rephrase the question, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have no intention of rephrasing the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to rephrase it. It's just that the witness needs to clear this up for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean, it's quite simple. You don't know from your knowledge, because you weren't there, whether these descriptions are accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously I was not present. However, according to the information that I had, I believe that this was all accurate and correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to look now, please, at P923. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me just summarise what it deals with. Omer Filipovic had asked for a postponement of the deadline to surrender the weapons. And what's called the Kljuc defence command that accepted the proposal on the basis that the seven captured soldiers and the deputy commander of the police station that was killed was handed over by 1700 hours. "We invite all citizens of Muslim nationality to hand in their weapons and fulfill their obligation. Should these conditions not be fulfilled and the weapons not handed in, or should some new military or other activity be undertaken, such weapons will be destroyed by the defence of the Kljuc Municipality." Now, you were there in Kljuc, and the situation was this, wasn't it, that negotiations went on with Omer Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the negotiations went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we look, now, please -- if you look at, please, 924 -- I've got it for the witness. This is a combat report for the 28th of May 1992. It's addressed to the command of the 30th Infantry division. If you look, please, at the item that I've highlighted for you. And it's on the second page of the English. "Because of the situation in Kljuc, the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Infantry Brigade was made fully combat ready as ordered. If the Muslims do not surrender their weapons by 27 May 1992 at 1200 hours, the battalion will carry out a mopping-up operation. To this battalion, combat group 2 has been attached and has been under our command since last night." Now, it's right, isn't it, Mr. Kalabic, that by the 28th of May, the whole of the Pudin Han area and other areas were surrounded by forces of the military?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Armed with guns, with tanks, with APCs, and infantry?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that there were no tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the information received at the crisis staff. And none of these units were a tank unit, so they couldn't have tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's leave aside the tanks for the moment. There was absolutely nothing the people in these villages could do against that army, was there? Was there, Mr. Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certain military formations. There were certain military formations which were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only arms, to your certain knowledge, of that of the army and the police that were held were mainly hunting rifles and a few light machine-guns. That was all, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the automatic rifles, the information was received only subsequently. There were a number of those, and there was also hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- the situation was this, wasn't it: That you, in conjunction with the army and the police, used these incidents as an excuse to drive the Muslims out?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The army arrived in Kljuc specifically because their young recruits on the way back from Knin had been attacked. 6 people were killed, and some 20 were injured. I don't know the exact numbers of those who were injured. And the army arrived because of that, not because they had other intentions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest this was a highly synchronised operation, and the excuse that was used was this deadline to surrender the arms and the seven captured men. And that's what happened, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether the operation was synchronised or not, I really wouldn't know. I don't know whether this was synchronised. There's nothing for me to know about that because the crisis staff did not engage in any detailed planning with this regard. It was indeed for the six or seven soldiers who were captured to be released. And the surrender of weapons was required to prevent a possible escalation of the conflict. Some people did indeed surrender their weapons, many didn't. A lot of weapons remained in the ground and will probably never be located or found again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I prefer to go on, Your Honour. I mean, I really still have quite a lot to cover with this witness. I mean, I don't mind. If this witness can come back here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to have a break now. This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, I can't deny -- the break is not yours or mine. It's everybody's. So we need to stop for 20 minutes and in the meantime Mr. Ackerman perhaps can converse with Ms. Korner to see how much you require for your re-examination. And if that is not feasible to combine with everything today, see what the solution is. We'll have a 20-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please, at part of a report for the 30th of May from the 1st Krajina Corps, Exhibit P936.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While he looks at that and thinks, have you come to some kind of an arrangement between you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman just told me five minutes' re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see there: "In the Velagici/Kula/Pudin Han area the 3rd Battalion is conducting mopping up of the Green Berets who are surrendering in droves. Some of the Green Berets have fled and are in hiding. One of our soldiers was killed." Were you aware that the Bosniaks, the Muslims, were surrendering in droves?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, were you also aware that the village of Pudin Han was shelled, and numerous civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received the information on the shelling later on. And we also received the information that there were some casualties during the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you describe as "some casualties"? How many people?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have that information at the time. And I still don't know to this very day how many people were killed in shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that those who fled towards Krasulje and then Hrustovo? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have that information. Well, they probably fled to various sites.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that on the 31st of May, the village of Zenica was attacked?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about the 31st of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I just correct. On the transcript, it says Zenica. It should be Sanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that on the 1st of June, the village of Prhovo was attacked? That's P-r-h-o-v-o.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received that information later on. Not I, but we were informed at the crisis staff about Prhovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also told that the men who had been taken from the village was from separated from the women and lined up along the road towards Peci?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the crisis staff, we did not receive such detailed information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you receive information that some civilians, people without arms, people under guard, were killed on that road?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information about casualties in that area we received later on. But this information was not thorough. We didn't have the full detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that women and children were killed during the attack on Prhovo?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we received that information later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you received this information, before we come to the Velagici killings, did you or anybody else on your crisis staff, to your knowledge, protest about this?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the crisis staff, we asked that civilians should not be touched and that they should be looked after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the police and the army who were involved in these operations took no notice of what you were asking. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked for that before and after the events in Prhovo. Despite our requests, things were done completely differently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's wrong, as that report says, to say that everything that happened happened in cooperation with the police, the army, and the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If something happens, as it did happen, information reached the crisis staff post-festin. So the crisis staff was never advised in advance of the things that might happen in the future. It was only after the event that the information reached us. Whether this was on the same day or one or two days after the events, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we come to the massacre at the Velagici school on the 1st of June. And you've described how you and Colonel Galic heard about it together. Do you agree that that was the most appalling war crime?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that stage, did you, in your capacity as a member of the assembly and as a member of the municipal crisis staff, say to anybody that "this must never happen and that there must be control of the troops"?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The control was required. However, the local authorities could not control what was going on in the army. In this particular case, Colonel Galic arrested certain people for whom he believed that they had done that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. And you know, don't you, that -- what happened to those people? They were released.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Colonel Galic said that they had to be arrested. That was his order, as a matter of fact, and the military investigation was initiated against them. What happened to these people after that, I don't know. I don't have any information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, weren't you interested to know what had happened to the perpetrators, the leaders, of this massacre?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, we did inquire, all of us from the crisis staff, as to what was happening and how far this had gone. And the answer was mostly that an investigation was carried out, and then a procedure was initiated before the military court and that the procedure was underway. That was the information that we received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't hear that the reason that these men were released was that representatives of the Kljuc Brigade appeared at court and said that unless the people who had been arrested were released, the entire Kljuc Brigade would leave the front line and could not guarantee that the lives of the prosecutor and the judges or the lives of anyone else would be safe? Did you ever hear that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that when attempts were made to resuscitate the prosecution in July of 1993, over a year later, that the investigating judge said that the investigation proceeding against the Lieutenant Amidzic had to be halted because the majority of the suspects were inaccessible to the prosecuting organs and because of a situation that arose when the president of the executive committee brought pressure that these people should not be prosecuted? Did you ever hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. And I believe that the president of the executive committee in Kljuc was not such an influential person to be able to put such pressure on a military court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to show you the document. I just want to move on. That wasn't the end of the killings, though, was it, in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war was on. What happened during the war --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about massacres, killings of unarmed people. Do you remember Biljani school?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of the Biljani school. I believe that at the time, I was -- I can't tell you where I was because I may not be right. But I was either on the front line or I was at the assembly. It was only upon my return to Kljuc that I heard that something like that had happened in Biljani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. There was another almost identical massacre on the 10th of July at the Biljani school, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I just said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crisis staff really did not have anything in their hands to be able to do anything but to insist for the perpetrators to be brought before the court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they weren't brought before the court either, were they?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't have the exact information on that. But I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's because, isn't it, that it was tacitly accepted that people, unarmed civilians, could be killed like this because they were not Serbs? That's the situation, isn't it, Mr. Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On several occasions at the crisis staff, we insisted, and you can see that from various documents, that the civilians should be protected, that they should not be touched. However, it did happen that some renegade soldiers would commit crimes unbeknown of the military command that they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but it wasn't just once that it happened in Kljuc, was it? It was over and over again. That's right, isn't it, Mr. Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the territory of Kljuc, there have been three such incidents. We have just mentioned all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But there were many more, not as large as Biljani or Velagici or Peci, but many, many other killings on a smaller scale of unarmed people, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war times, things did happen. Cases like that did happen. However, a lot of people in Kljuc belonged to military groups that were not part of the regular army, so there were groups who just followed events looking for room to plunder and to get rich. That's why people, innocent people, were killed, those people who never participated in the war, nor they ever intended to participate in it. Some indictments were raised against some people. How far has that gone, I don't know. I don't have the information on that. So there were killings of the Muslim population, of the Serbian population. It all depended on who was it who intended to plunder or loot property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was every way that any of these so-called paramilitaries could have been stopped by the army and the police who were there in force in Kljuc, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody had power in Kljuc. Neither me, nor Jovo Banjac, nor anybody who was on the crisis staff. Nobody could vouch for their own safety, let alone the safety of anybody else. You will find it in the documents that the police was often asked to protect people and buildings, to prevent these things from happening. And the police was very efficient in Velecevo [Realtime transcript read in error "Velagici"], Zgon, and Dubocani. In those villages, the police was particularly efficient and they managed to protect both the people and the property there, and this was done at the request of the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at some stage, the police were doing what you wanted; but most of the time, they weren't. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to this type of protection that I've just mentioned, in these villages it was carried out properly. The police had its own hierarchy, and the Kljuc police was subordinated to the CSB in Banja Luka, and the Kljuc police --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that, and you don't need to tell us that again, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 77.1 shouldn't be Velagici, it should be Velecevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Velecevo. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's right. But anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I would be grateful that there are no further interruptions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I intend to correct the transcript any time it's wrong and misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and I will let you do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to show you P1012. I'll show the part I'm interested in from there onward. This is the report of the SJB to the assembly. I want you to look, please, under paragraph 5, page 5 in the English, "knowledge gained through investigations." "All intelligence work has shown that the Muslim TO was primarily organised for defence operations. Their patrol guarded only the entrance into their own villages, and the defence system was positioned on the edge of and within the villages themselves." Do you accept that the police themselves knew that they were under no threat from the Muslims? No, don't -- just answer the question, please, Mr. Kalabic.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that. I saw that there were no barricades on the public roads, so I assume if there were barricades somewhere, that those were the villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the bottom of that page, under the pretext, I should read this: "That they were merely preparing to protect their villages and homes. They were preparing their defence system and organised a Muslim TO. All of our findings point to the fact that the Muslim TO was primarily set up for defence purposes." And then: "Investigation through operational work, establish meetings held in Prijedor and Sanski Most, adopted a decision to commence armed rebellion." And then at the bottom of this paragraph, this: "The attacks they launched on the 27th of May 1992 gave proper cause to the members of the BH Serbian Republic Army to settle accounts by taking determined action against the perpetrators of and participants in these acts." Mr. Kalabic, do you accept, as I put to you about an hour ago, that those incidents were used as an excuse to attack and drive out the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That could not be taken as an excuse. It couldn't be accepted. At least not as far as I knew, although with respect to this information, the crisis staff never received the information in this form. It was addressed to the public security centre, and I never had an opportunity to hear it in this form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in effect what you're telling us is that the municipal crisis staff got no information at all about anything. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't say it didn't get any information about anything. Yes, it did get information, but it got it in the form and quantity that those who were transmitting the information thought necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you go to, please, paragraph Roman numeral number 7, "Kljuc SJB operations." Page 8 on the English. "Participation in combat activities. SJB officers took part in all the combat activities and mopping-up of the terrain in order to arrest the participants in the armed rebellion and to find weapons. We suffered no casualties in these actions apart from a slight self-inflicted wound. All operations were conducted in cooperation with the command of the 30th Division. We noticed on that occasion that apart from the units in the first line of attack, the rest of the units are prone to looting and torching abandoned houses." And then it goes on to the processing. Before we come to the processing of prisoners, could you then go to under paragraph 3 "finding and confiscating weapons." And you'll find the next highlighted section, which is on page 9 in the English. "The SJB has collected in accordance with the decision adopted by the crisis staff 270 registered hunting rifles, 200 registered handguns. These weapons have been stored and a record has been filed. The following unregistered weapons were also confiscated: 100 automatic rifles, 9 semi-automatic rifles, 9 submachine-guns, 45 hunting rifles, a 60-millimetre mortar, 40 handguns, 20 various automatic rifles, around 90 old-fashioned pistols, 20 self-activating grenades, and a large quantity of ammunition of various types and calibres." Would you agree, Mr. Kalabic, that the Muslim resistance was hardly well armed?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could say that because this report shows this was so. If it's really true that all the rifles and other weapons were really found and handed over to the public security station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally the subject of prisoners. I want you to look, please, at Exhibit P1033. This was a response from Mr. Kondic to the Serbian Republic for information in respect of prisons in Kljuc. "No camps, prisons, or collection centres in our municipality. We send all our prisoners to the Manjaca prisoner-of-war camp in Dobrinja." There are on that list, aren't there, attached to this letter 1.100 -- I'm sorry, yes. That's 1.163 people listed? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All or most of those people in Manjaca were civilians, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that most of these people were on Omer Filipovic's list and that they were deployed in military formations. Such a list was found; that is, Omer Filipovic did have this list in his bag. And it stated who the commanders were, who belonged to what unit, what platoon, and I think that this is in question here. But this is the first time I'm looking at the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 86 was a man born in 1934. Number 83 was a man born in 1934. And scattered throughout these lists are people who were born around that time. Are you saying that in your genuine belief, all these people who were sent to Manjaca were part of the TO? The Muslim TO?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I want to say is what I've already said. I think that most of the people on this list were, that they were on the list of the army formed by Mr. Filipovic. I'm saying the largest number. I cannot assert anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't think about going to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you think you ought to check that all these huge numbers of Muslims who, to your knowledge, were locked up in Manjaca were properly there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not have this possibility, I think, because Manjaca and Dobrinja is a big military barracks, and probably even had I thought of doing this, I would not have been allowed entry or I would have had to undergo a lengthy procedure. This was a military issue. But at the crisis staff, I and others insisted with the military commanders that prisoners should be treated humanely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you think perhaps you ought to check whether that was actually happening?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that time now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they weren't only being held at Manjaca, were they, prisoners? For a time, at least, they were being held at the police station in Kljuc. You knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly they passed through the police station. There, the police carried out certain interrogation, identification. And then sent these people on to Manjaca, to the military prison camp. And this was done by the police in agreement with the military command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Nikola Mlakic school? That was a prison as well, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no prison in Kljuc, so at the time that groups of people are questioned, and a lot of people came and gave themselves in, the questioning was carried out there. And after the interrogation, they were taken to Manjaca. Of course, neither I nor the crisis staff participated in this. It was the military command and the police who were in charge of that. It was our task only to ask that these people be treated humanely, and I have to say that Mr. Banjac, on several occasions, reacted quite strongly towards both of these parties so that we did what we could to help those people and to have things be as easy for them as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Nikola Mlakic school was very close to the municipal building where you held the meetings of the crisis staff. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's one of the neighbouring buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were fully aware, weren't you, that people were being beaten and beaten to death in that building?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not know that in this form. But whenever we noticed that something was happening which was not in accordance with normal human behaviour, we intervened, both with the police and with the military command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you call something that isn't in accordance with "normal human behaviour"?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If someone set out to beat someone, then of course we would respond and say that such things must not happen, although in spite of our reactions, such things did happen quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The school came under the control of the municipal assembly; and when it wasn't meeting, under the control of the crisis staff, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand how the school could have been under the control of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The school premises were owned or however you like to put it, run by the assembly. It wasn't a private school, was it? It was a public school.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, all institutions and all companies were public, state-owned companies, and schools.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the point that I'm trying to make, Mr. Kalabic, is that you, the crisis staff, could have simply told the police they could not use this building as a prison.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This did not last for a long time. And I think the crisis staff contributed to the fact that people were no longer interrogated in the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, do you - looking back now - think that you have any responsibility for what happened in Kljuc during that period of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did my best, and I think I contributed quite a lot to peace being maintained in Kljuc for a long time. Further, I think that together with the other people in the crisis staff, I contributed quite a lot to putting a stop to all the negative things that were happening on the territory of Kljuc Municipality. And this is how I see my own actions in respect of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you wouldn't accept that you or your fellow members of the crisis staff had any responsibility for what happened to the Muslims and the Croats in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have done more than we did, but I really did do my best to do as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Kalabic. You are not obliged, until we tell you to, to answer any question any way that you could possibly incriminate yourself. So if you think that by answering this question, or any other question, you could expose yourself to criminal proceedings, you can ask us not to -- to exempt you from answering that question, and then we will decide what to do. But if you think you are free and can answer the question without any such problems, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman, you have redirect, I suppose? Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, in the course of the examination today, you've heard a lot and talked a lot about some of the unfortunate events that happened in the Kljuc Municipality, killings, things of that nature. At the end of your testimony yesterday, I asked you two questions and preceded them with "bad things happened in Kljuc Municipality." The first question I asked you was did any of those things happen because of the ARK Crisis Staff or because Radoslav Brdjanin or the ARK Crisis Staff directed them to happen. The second question I asked you was could Radoslav Brdjanin or the ARK Crisis Staff have prevented any of those incidents or events. Is your answer today any different from the answer you gave yesterday with regard to those questions?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I abide by my reply of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for coming. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Janu, do you have any questions? Judge Janu from the Czech Republic has got some questions for you, sir. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Kalabic, I have just one question for you. You are from Kljuc. You were in quite a high position in politics. Could you assist the Chamber in giving us the names of the most dangerous Muslim extremists from the Kljuc Municipality, of course.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was exclusively Mr. Omer Filipovic, and that everything revolved around him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So just this one name?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The others, for the most part, acted on his orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Taya, any questions? Judge Taya from Japan also has a question for you, Mr. Kalabic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: I have for a question why Mr. Filipovic is so dangerous, according to you.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He waged a policy in Kljuc, in my view, which led to the escalation that took place. And he carried out everything that he received on a daily basis from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what happened to Omer Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information, or rather we, at the crisis staff in the municipality, received information according to which Omer Filipovic died in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How did he die in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the explanation of how he died, nobody gave us that information, although we did request it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So even to date, you are not aware of how Omer Filipovic died?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Even to date, of course, I don't have this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Kalabic, for having come over. This is the end of your testimony here. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, anything else before we rise?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's back to Mr. Ackerman's new and exciting list. It states on it that Mr. Whatever his name is, Bojinovic, number 17, may or may not be coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's soft.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like to know when we're going to be told whether he will be coming and if he's not coming, who's replacing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's a footnote there, and that's the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: . Yes, right, that's -- Your Honour, I'm afraid that's not good enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I knew that no matter what I did it wouldn't be good enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it if he was in a position to tell us today, he would tell us today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm anxious to avoid is that we're told on the Monday prior to the Wednesday that number 17 is being replaced by somebody completely different and someone who may be a major witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I have an undertaking from you that by Thursday before the beginning -- before the 26th of November you will let us all know whether Mr. Bojinovic is coming over or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, as yet, we've had no names of any military expert, police expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's true as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'd like to know if we're any further on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're no further on that one. So far, all of our efforts have met with failure in both respects, and chances are we're not going to have an expert of either kind, but I can't tell you exactly yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now we have a short break of a few days during which Mr. Ackerman and your team will be conducting your own on-site inquiries, and I'm saying this in public because I want to avoid the impression that we will not be sitting for a few days for some other reason. These days are important for the Defence to reorganise its efforts. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's absolutely correct. It's an absolutely important mission that we have to undertake in Bosnia, and I'm sorry to delay the trial, but it doesn't really delay the trial. It makes it more efficient. When we come back from there, I think we will have a final witness list and a final estimate for the Court on when we'll complete the case. We intend to try to reduce witness numbers during this trip, and I think we'll succeed in that. I think Your Honours will be pleased with the results when we return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And maybe you'll find a military expert there. So I thank you, and we will all meet again after your return from Bosnia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of November, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
